topic: Benjamin-Plus: Measured Token-Efficiency Skill for Coding Agents

key_points: Primary subject: JetBrains-published MIT skill, 330 stars / 14 forks, created 2026-08-17, last pushed 2026-08-27.
Claims up to -18% cost and -22% tokens per task with quality unchanged; headline v6 result is -17.9% median paired cost (p=0.005), -16.7% on totals.
Five rules: (1) recon in one pass, (2) keyhole reads, (3) probe environment once, (4) green means the task's own check, (5) polling is a step.
Injected payload is ~745 tokens (v6), ~3KB integration cost; distribution is injection ONLY.

Measured head-to-head: injected saves (-17.9% median), installed as a discoverable skill folder saves nothing net (-0.5%, n.s.) because agents burn a median 3 steps finding SKILL.md with 73% path misses.
External validation: Java SWE-bench, Codex CLI gpt-5.6-luna, 675 paired replicas -> -4.4% cost [-7.5,-1.5] p=0.003, solve rate unchanged p=0.22, tool calls -20%.
Method: paired A/B on 80 SkillsBench tasks, Claude Code 2.1.201 in Docker, Sonnet 5 low effort; Wilcoxon on paired deltas; adoption verified 80/80 treated vs 0/80 control.

Honesty caveats: v5 same setup measured only -10.0% median cost (p=0.169); the control arm drifted +10.5% between days while treatment stayed flat, so savings scale with baseline bloat (-10% to -18%).
Open issues show real friction in rule examples: 'find_spec probe is not robust for dotted module names' (#17) and shell-semantics fixes (#18).

Primary/authoritative source. JetBrains-published, MIT-licensed 'token-efficiency skill' for coding agents. Repo created 2026-08-17, last push 2026-08-27; 330 stars / 14 forks / 2 open issues as of 2026-10-01 (via GitHub search API; 5 commits, 1 contributor, no releases, no CI).

Core thesis: 'An agent pays twice for every clumsy lookup: once for the step itself, and again every time the growing conversation gets re-read.' The skill changes how the agent looks things up and waits, never what it builds.

Five habits: (1) Recon in one pass (chain probes with ';' and label sections; sample two examples before copying a convention); (2) Look through a keyhole (| head -50 / offset+limit on inspection only — truncated data you will transform corrupts output); (3) Probe the environment once (check every dependency in one command, install missing in one go); (4) Green means the task's own check (the task-named verification command is the definition of done; an 'environmental' failure is still yours; same check failing twice means the approach is wrong; when it passes, stop); (5) Polling is a step (wait in >=30s slices, never re-poll at 1s).

Headline claim: 'Measured: up to -18% cost and -22% tokens per task, quality unchanged.' README states savings scale with baseline bloat and quotes ~-10% to ~-18% cost depending on how bloated sessions run.
Deliberate distribution stance: 'injected, it saves (-17.9% cost median); as a discoverable skill folder, it saves nothing (-0.5%, n.s.; agents burned steps just finding SKILL.md). So: inject.'

Guardrails written into the payload: 'efficiency never outranks correctness', keyhole rules 'apply to inspection, never to ingestion', 'never build a verification harness, test suite, or checker the task didn't ask for', 'close with at most two lines', 'no victory laps'.

Install surfaces: Claude Code SessionStart hook (matcher 'startup|resume|clear|compact' -> cat ~/.benjamin-plus/injected-instruction.md), per-project 'cat ... >> CLAUDE.md', Codex CLI '>> ~/.codex/AGENTS.md', or append to any system prompt (~3 KB total).
Closest competitor on positioning: 'always-on token-efficiency skill' for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, Cline. 473 stars, created 2026-07-03.
Claims ~31% lower bill on average (-17% to -54% by session type) and -30% to -81% output on real Sonnet 5 runs.
Per-session-type numbers: output-heavy advice/planning -81% output / -54% bill; code change + tests (nestjs/nest, 1673 files) -49% / -22%; read-heavy comprehension -30% / -17%.
Scope is broader than benjamin-plus: it also compresses the agent's own replies, docs, commit/handoff text, and test counts (<=10 tests per session), not just lookups.
Offers levels: on / lite / ultra (telegraphic chat) / off, and per-project vs global install via a curl installer.
Explicit guardrail: concision applies to output, never to reasoning; correctness, critical test coverage, and verbatim code/errors are off-limits.
Same delivery insight: a skill body is on-demand, so it uses a SessionStart hook or always-loaded context file (AGENTS.md / rule files) to be always-on.
Narrower, tool-level skill (30 stars, MIT): minimize waste in tool use, file reading, and data processing at the source.
Prescribes jq/yq/awk over dump-and-read, ast-grep/rg over broad text search, git --stat/--name-only summary-first, quiet flags + NO_COLOR, hash-based change detection, coreutils over Python.
Ships a sunset notice: it exists only because current agents have not internalized efficient tool use, and it will be discontinued as models improve.
Distributed through native marketplaces: Claude Code plugin marketplace, Gemini CLI extensions, plus .codex/.opencode INSTALL docs.

Discipline-first alternative (17 stars, GPL-3.0, v1.17.0, actively pushed 2026-09-20): compresses invalid context/reasoning/output but pairs it with the Ten Principles of Wei Liaozi for permission boundaries.

Core contribution is a task-mode decision table: seven modes (simple Q&A, small code edit, multi-file task, large-material summary, major architecture change, ...) each with its own toolchain, output format, and token budget.
Targets Reasonix / Codex CLI / OpenCode / Hermes / Cline; distributed on GitHub plus ClawHub.
Useful contrast: benjamin-plus is five mechanical rules; zerotoken is a mode-selection framework plus behavioral order.
Strong independent mechanism explanation that a review can cite: chat completions are stateless, so cost ~ transcript size x turns, and a file read on turn 3 of a 40-turn run is paid 37 more times.
Model-free wire-cost harness: 36 scripted tool calls, 37 turns -> baseline 4,157,949 bytes (~1,039,487 tokens), 112,377 bytes/turn; optimization pass halved it to ~517k tokens.
Concrete levers that generalize: shrink tool schemas (5,193 -> 4,556 bytes, ~160 tokens/turn, with a build-time byte budget), and re-reading/re-searching is pure residue.
Documents an 'optimization' that made the run 10% worse until the harness caught it - evidence that token work needs measurement, not intuition.
Hacker News signal for the angle: 'Show HN: I nerfed our coding agents on purpose' (27 pts, 10 comments, 2026-06-05) and 'Half the tokens for the same 36 tool calls' (app.nz, 2026-08-07).
No HN thread exists for benjamin-plus itself (Algolia nbHits ~2 for related terms), so the article faces little direct discussion competition.

v6 FINAL (2026-08-16, job bp6-final), 80 paired SkillsBench tasks, Sonnet 5, low effort, Claude Code 2.1.201 in Docker: cost -17.9% median paired (p=0.005) and -16.7% on totals; turns -20.0% (p=0.001); total tokens -21.9% (p=0.001); cache reads -23.9% (p=0.001); output tokens -21.2% (p=0.007); code written -13.3% (p=0.006); wall-clock -15.6% (p=0.018); fresh input -7.8% (p=0.125, not significant).

Quality: no difference detected — 7 better / 5 worse / 68 tie, sign test p=0.77, mean verifier reward 0.362 -> 0.392. Document is explicit: 'not powered as an equivalence test — large effects ruled out, small ones not.'

Honesty note on effect size: the v5 same-day run (bp-final, 2026-08-15) measured only -10.0% median cost (p=0.169, NOT significant). Between the two days the CONTROL arm drifted +10.5% median / +20.5% totals while the treated arm stayed flat (-3.0%). The skill is framed as a 'session-cost variance clamp' whose measured saving scales with how expensive the baseline happens to run.

v5 archive: -11.5% code written (p=0.012) and -13.9% wall-clock (p=0.039) were the statistically solid wins; medians and totals disagreed (arm totals flat at +0.6% cost) because 'the skill wins the middle of the distribution and gives some of it back on trap-task tails.'

Install-method finding (external, decisive): Java SWE-bench, Codex CLI, gpt-5.6-luna, 225 instances x 3 replicas (675 paired replicas) — hook-injected benjamin was the only arm significantly cheaper at -4.4% cost [-7.5, -1.5], p=0.003, solve rate unchanged (p=0.22), tool calls -20%; skill-folder install saved nothing net (-0.5% n.s.) because fetching SKILL.md cost a median 3 steps with 73% path misses.

v6 added exactly one rule, 'Polling is a step', after Java SWE-bench traces showed 45.8% of the treated arm's agent steps were polls, 3,982 of them at sub-5-second yields — a waste pool the v5 rules never touched.

Mechanical adoption proof: payload reached the model in 80/80 treated runs vs 0/80 controls; labelled probe chains 10 -> 102 commands; batched dependency probes 7/80 -> 22/80 trials; Read calls 144 -> 57; Read with offset/limit 20% -> 28%.

Program spend disclosed: ~$153 across 254 billed trials (bp1 $14.94, bp2 ~$8.6, bp3 $49.04, bp4 $9.08, bp5 $6.83, bp-final $64.40). Design lesson: 'quality guards are not free' — the winning config deleted more rules than it added; every guard (v2 check rigor, v3 check-to-file) generated 'verification whales' that erased savings elsewhere.

Context: JetBrains runs a public paired-A/B series against third-party 'token saver' add-ons and publishes the measured delta. Part 3 = ponytail skill: advertised -54% code / -22% tokens / -20% cost / -27% time; measured -15% code, -10.3% cost (p=0.004, cheaper on 46 of 80 pairs), -11% time, no quality difference detected.

Explicitly the first tool in the series with a statistically solid cost saving ('roughly 10% cheaper on this workload is defensible; ponytail saves you 10% is not'), with the caveat that a bootstrap interval on the median just touches zero.
Establishes the pattern Benjamin-Plus is judged against: vendor-published numbers typically land at a quarter to a half of the advertised figure.

Part 2 = rtk ('Rust Token Killer') CLI proxy: advertised 60-90% token reduction; measured +7.6% MORE expensive at low reasoning effort (p=0.004) on 80 clean pairs, and flat at high effort (+0.1%, p=0.99). Setup: Claude Code 2.1.201, claude-sonnet-5, SkillsBench 86/87 tasks, 425 billed trials, ~$320.

Mechanism lesson that bounds benjamin-plus's addressable surface: the Bash hook only ever sees ~33% of Bash calls (~20% of tool-result chars); Claude Code's built-in Read/Grep bypass the hook entirely, and cached re-reads bill at a tenth of the price.
rtk's own dashboard reported 96.2 million tokens 'saved' (99.8% of everything it touched) in the same run where the measured bill went up — 'the scoreboard is grading its own homework.'

Part 1 = caveman skill: advertised -65% output tokens; measured -8.5% output tokens and ~-10% cost at absolute best (forced activation = best case), 82 paired tasks, p=0.82, ~$106 / 240 billed trials. Verdict: 'Safe, honest about style, oversold on savings.'

Why the 65% never reaches your bill: agentic output is dominated by code, diffs, tool-call payloads and exact error strings, which the skill preserves byte-exact by design; only narration between tool calls is compressible.
Same lab, same method, same harness as benjamin-plus — this is the credibility context a review must state (the vendor turns the method on its own product).

Vendor motivation, first-party: JetBrains' own AI development expenses increased roughly 10x in the first half of 2026; most of its developers use between three and five AI tools in a given month; they hit 150 Claude Code seats and moved to an API-usage-based Enterprise plan 'that's when costs really took off.'
Frames benjamin-plus as an in-house cost-control artifact in the same program as the third-party skill benchmark series, not a standalone product launch.
Independent hands-on review, published 2026-08-23, rated 4/5 gears (quality 4, docs 4, setup 5, value 4, ecosystem fit 3). Tested on macOS 26.5.2 / bash 3.2 / Node 24.13.1 / Claude Code CLI 2.1.152.

Calls it 'the most honest eval write-up in this category' and independently reconciles the metadata: 225 instances x 3 replicas = the '675 paired replicas' the README cites, and the token claim (745) matches a chars/4 heuristic on the 2,996-byte payload (749) almost exactly.

Hand verification: fresh clone = 2.1 MB / 11 files outside .git; 'bash hooks/sessionstart.sh | wc -l' = 55 lines, exit 0, executable bit set as cloned; 'shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS.txt' = 8 of 8 checksums OK.

Critical findings: the README's 'Reproducing' section reproduces nothing (gen_instruction.py, compare.py, adoption.py, mediators.py, LAB-NOTES.md, winning-strats.md are all absent from the public repo; no eval code ships), so the headline is trust in a document, not a rerunnable harness; and 'npx skills add JetBrains/benjamin-plus-skill' exits 1 with 'No valid skills found' despite RULESET.md carrying full SKILL.md frontmatter (deliberate per the README's inject-only thesis).

Skill-registry listing (Development community) that mirrors the README verbatim. Notably weak on installation: it records only the repository, not the path inside it, so it gives no exact command — a concrete instance of the 'agents burn steps finding SKILL.md' problem the upstream payload cites as its reason for injection-only distribution.
Listed at 272 stars as of 2026-08-27, illustrating how fast the third-party numbers drift versus the live repo (330 today).

Business-judgment page (tracked from 2026-08-17, updated 2026-09-07): verdict 'Worth trying' — official JetBrains release, stars growing (283 -> 298 -> 311 across snapshots), but 'repeat use and payment not yet verified' and its explicit unknown is that the 'injection method and applicability need further validation.'
Useful as the demand-side framing: cost control for coding agents is becoming a necessity, and the gap is that users optimize prompts/models/usage frequency but lack a systematic solution.

Directory metadata cross-check: 311 stars / 13 forks / MIT / last commit 2026-08-18, language Shell 100%, 1 contributor with 5 commits. Corroborates that the project is a very small, single-author artifact (DenisSergeevitch) rather than infrastructure.
Confirms the repo sits in curated-directory feeds (FOSSY, Cult of Claude, ainotes) without a skills.sh registry presence.

Summary source agreeing on the mechanics and on the honest range: 'measured cost reductions ranging from about 10% to 18% depending on baseline behavior, with unchanged quality in its reported evaluation', plus the cross-platform Java SWE-bench measurement with reduced cost and tool calls.

Notes it is 'intended to be injected into an agent's instructions rather than installed as a discoverable skill' and was surfaced via a GitHub-trending video roundup (#46) — evidence of discovery momentum outside the AI-cost niche.

angles: Measurement-first framing: most token-efficiency skills are vibes; benjamin-plus ships a paired A/B with p-values, an adoption check (80/80 vs 0/80), and an honesty section admitting a non-significant earlier run. That candor is the story.

The delivery finding is the most actionable and least obvious part: injecting a ~745-token payload saves, while installing the same skill as a discoverable folder saves nothing (-0.5% n.s.) because agents spend median 3 steps hunting SKILL.md with 73% path misses. 'Don't install it, inject it.'

Savings scale with baseline bloat, not with task: -10% on a lean-baseline day vs -18% against a bloated baseline; the skill behaves like a session-cost variance clamp. Anyone quoting a single number is over-claiming.
Polling as the hidden cost center: 45.8% of agent steps in the Java run were polls, 3,982 at sub-5s. That reframes 'token efficiency' as a scheduling problem, not a prompt-wording problem.

Where the honest limits are: quality was NOT powered as an equivalence test (80 pairs only rules out large effects), medians and totals disagree (-17.9% median vs -16.7% totals; v5 median -10.0% but totals +0.6%), and open issue #17 shows the dependency-probe rule misfires on dotted module names.

Head-to-head: benjamin-plus (5 mechanical lookup rules, ~745 tokens, cost-focused) vs token-diet (broader output+artifact compression, -31% avg bill, tiered lite/ultra levels) vs undefdev/token-efficiency (tooling-level jq/rg/git habits, self-declared sunset notice) vs zerotoken (7-mode decision framework plus discipline constraints). Different bets: steps+context vs output volume vs tool hygiene vs process order.

Mechanism explainer to include: stateless chat APIs make cost = transcript size x turns; the expensive thing is the residue work leaves in the transcript, which is why 'keyhole reads' and 'batching' work at all.

The measurement is the product. Benjamin-Plus is one of the very few vendor-published agent skills shipping paired A/B receipts with a caveat section that argues against its own headline; the review should lead with the method, not the -17.9%.

Inject, don't install is the load-bearing finding — and it generalizes far beyond this repo. A discoverable SKILL.md cost a median 3 steps with 73% path misses, so 'discovery' was a net loss on a 745-token payload. This is the sharpest counter-argument in circulation to 'move everything into skills'.

Savings scale with baseline bloat: the honest range is -10% to -18% cost, and the skill behaves as a session-cost variance clamp (control drifted +10.5% between run days while the treated arm stayed flat). Any headline number is a property of the baseline, not the skill.

Medians vs totals is a real distinction, not pedantry: in the v5 run the skill was cheaper on the median task but flat in aggregate because a tail of hard 'trap' tasks made it work longer. Buyers budgeting a monthly bill should read totals.

The trust boundary is the biggest caveat: the repo ships no eval code, and the 'Reproducing' section names four scripts plus LAB-NOTES.md and winning-strats.md that do not exist publicly. The headline is trust in a well-written document from one contributor with a 5-commit history.

The ruleset is a living artifact, not a frozen claim: 17 community issues in three weeks, six shell-semantics bugs fixed in merged PR #18 (which itself grows the payload 788 -> ~899 tokens), and the rule-semantics fix from issue #4 still unmerged — so 'the file you inject in October is not the file that was benchmarked in August'.

Keyhole reads are conditional on file size. Community issue #9 shows the rule can add a step with zero context savings on a small file (1 'cat' versus measure-then-slice on a 65-line file) — a reviewer should state when the rule misfires rather than only praising it.

Position it on the measured-premium ledger: caveman advertised -65% and measured -8.5%; rtk advertised 60-90% and measured +7.6% cost; ponytail advertised -54% code / -20% cost and measured -15% / -10.3%. Benjamin-Plus is the same lab turning the same method on its own product, which is why its numbers are the most credible in the category.

The skill-index tax is the framing that makes injection make sense: a measured 78-skill registry cost 8,260 tokens of context before the user typed anything, paid whether or not a skill ever fires. Injection is 'resident but tiny'; discovery is 'cheap-looking but per-turn'.

Cross-platform reality check: the effect shrinks to -4.4% cost on Java SWE-bench with Codex CLI (675 paired replicas), still significant, still with -20% tool calls. A review should not promise the SkillsBench figure to a Codex or Java team.

Correctness guards are the interesting engineering story: five rules in, six rules' worth of guardrails included ('efficiency never outranks correctness', keyhole for inspection never ingestion, never build an unrequested verification harness). The upstream lab's own lab notes say quality guards generated 'verification whales' that erased savings — this tension is the most transferable lesson for anyone writing their own skill.

Adoption honesty: star count is small and single-author (330 stars / 14 forks / 1 contributor / no releases / no CI) and directory listings already disagree on the number (272 / 298 / 311 / 330 across sources), so popularity should not be the argument for adopting it.

Note on existing coverage: a sibling slug 'benjamin-plus-token-efficiency-skill-2026' was already researched and published (2026-09-21) by this same pipeline with very similar framing. This brief targets the distinct short slug/Keyword 'benjamin plus skill' (230 est. volume, kd 6) and should differentiate by leading with the v6 vs v5 honesty note, the merged PR #18 payload growth, the absent eval code, and the wider measured-premium ledger — not by re-telling the five habits.
